A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 rows toward higher y, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials yet. The starting network scored 0.000 on both seeds. Its default recipe makes only about 32 PPO updates (131k steps at 4096 steps per update), which is very little for a 257-way action space where every placement has to be exactly right. My first guess is that the budget is spent badly: too few updates and too much reuse of each sample. Fewer epochs buy more samples, and smaller rollouts give more updates. A second possible problem is the action head. Its max/min/avg pooling over a brick's footprint cannot easily check each cell in the footprint against the landing layer, which an exact build needs (equal heights, target filled at that layer, gaps left empty). This round separates the two: A changes only the recipe. B and C add a footprint-kernel convolution head, using the recipe from A (B) and a more aggressive one-epoch recipe (C).

### Round 2
Every trial so far scored 0, in training as well as on dev. Changing the head, the number of PPO epochs, the sample count and the learning rate made no difference, so the results don't rank any of these ideas. Exact success means the agent must make no wrong placement and must also choose DONE at the right moment. I see two likely blockers. (1) DONE trap: early in training, a random DONE ends the episode and loses the shaped reward still to come, so DONE gets pushed down everywhere. Exact builds are rare, so the +1 bonus is almost never seen, and the agent keeps placing bricks after the build is complete. (2) Wrong inductive bias: a good placement means the brick lands at layer h and fills cells that are missing at h. Flattening the layers into channels makes the network learn this indexing implicitly. This round tests a DONE logit tied to how good the best placement is, and a weight-shared network that scores each layer separately with footprint kernels and then combines the layers.

### Round 3
All 6 trials scored exactly 0, both on dev and in training (train_success_last10pct = 0). That held across two heads, two recipes, a coupled DONE logit and a per-layer scorer. Seed noise cannot explain a floor this flat, so something basic is likely wrong. Every design so far scores action (t, y, x) from local conv features at cell (y, x). If this world's action indexing or anchor convention differs from the description, which the task hints is possible, no local head can learn the mapping. Next round should test spatial-layout robustness with heads that can learn any feature-to-action map: a conv trunk plus a dense flattened head, a transformer with learned position embeddings, and a pure MLP. Recipe and DONE changes alone did not help. If any of these scores above 0, round 4 should refine that one.

### Round 4
After 9 trials every result is 0, on dev and on train success, including the baseline. Changing the recipe (epochs, lr, gamma, entropy, sample count) did not help. Neither did footprint heads, the coupled DONE logit, layer-wise scorers, attention or a layout-free MLP. Even training rollouts with sampled actions never produced an exact build. That points to something systematic and fits the warning that this world may not behave as described. One possibility is that the action indexing doesn't match the observation layout: transposed axes, flipped axes or a shifted anchor. Translation-equivariant local heads could never learn that. Dense heads and the MLP could in principle, but they learn slowly. With one round left, I'm betting on one architecture that tolerates a convention mismatch. It feeds the action mask (which lives in action space) into the network as input. A wide 5x5 output conv covers anchor offsets. Learned logit maps are combined across identity, flip and transpose variants. The three candidates differ in recipe or in adding a dense path.

## Trial it ended with
name: Symmetry-mixture head + mask input
hypothesis: Inputs gain the action mask (reshaped into per-type maps) and coordinate channels. A 5x5 output conv produces per-type logit maps for 5 variants (identity, flip-y, flip-x, rotate-180, transpose), which are summed. Training can strengthen whichever variant matches this world's action convention, and the 5x5 kernel covers anchor offsets. Recipe as r1c1. If a hidden layout mismatch is the blocker, success should rise above 0. A score of 0 refutes the idea.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 4 suspects a spatial misalignment: "the action indexing doesn't match the observation layout: transposed axes, flipped axes or a shifted anchor." Round 3 likewise asks whether "this world's action indexing or anchor convention differs." That is the right kind of change, a spatial offset between what is observed and where actions land. The text never says the target channels are rolled 4 rows toward higher y with wraparound. Its 5x5 kernel also covers only small offsets.
